extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court, federal courts, PTO, patent attorneys, policymakers, and biotechnology stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical criteria for determining whether DNA-related inventions (e.g., isolated genomic DNA, cDNA, methods) qualify as patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, with emphasis on product-of-nature and preemption doctrines. The guidance addresses how courts should evaluate structural changes, synthesis vs. isolation, utility, public-interest concerns, and reliance on PTO/congressional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 subject-matter categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §101 an inventor may obtain a patent on 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline statutory scope of patentable subject matter; all further exceptions and limitations (product-of-nature, laws of nature, abstract ideas) are applied against this statutory baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / law-of-nature exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable — such 'manifestations of ... nature' are 'free to all men and reserved exclusively to none.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A discovery of something that exists in nature (even if difficult to discover) does not by itself make it patentable. Examples cited: a new mineral or plant found in the wild is not patentable. This exception limits §101 regardless of effort or ingenuity expended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different (Chakrabarty) test for modified natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: A modified natural substance may be patent-eligible if it is 'markedly different' from its natural predecessor in characteristics and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed subject has distinctive chemical structure/identity and new properties or utilities not present in nature (Chakrabarty). If the modification creates a new substance with new characteristics and significant utility, it supports eligibility. Compare with Funk Brothers where mere discovery without alteration was insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption inquiry / 'significantly more' (Mayo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim (method or composition) would have the practical effect of preempting all uses of an underlying natural law or product; a claim must amount to 'significantly more' than the natural law/product itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether granting the patent would 'tie up' future use of the natural substance or law. For method claims, require additional elements sufficient so the patent in practice is more than a patent on the natural law. For compositions, if isolation/changes are just prerequisites to use, treating them as inventions risks preemption and thus invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere act of extracting or 'isolating' a naturally occurring substance from its environment does not convert it into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation typically causes only minor structural changes inherent to removal; these incidental consequences do not render the substance 'human-made' for §101 purposes. Compare with historical refusals to treat isolated elements/minerals as new 'manufactures.' If isolation were sufficient, it could effectively preempt the underlying natural product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of human manipulation / synthesis criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed subject results from significant human manipulation or synthesis rather than mere extraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substances created by synthesis or substantial human-directed alteration (e.g., cDNA synthesized from mRNA, recombinant constructs) are likelier to be patent-eligible because they are human-made and do not risk preempting the natural raw materials. By contrast, products that are only extracted with minimal change are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural / chemical-difference assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claimed composition has meaningful chemical or structural differences from the natural product (e.g., whether the isolated portion 'ever exists as a separate molecule in the body').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physical changes such as bond-breaking, contiguity of sequence, or other structural transformations. Substantial structural change that yields a different chemical identity supports eligibility; trivial or incidental changes attendant to isolation do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility comparison as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the utility of the claimed (isolated or modified) molecule to the native, naturally occurring molecule; greater or new utility can support eligibility in some views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Moore's concurrence suggested isolated DNA could be eligible only if it had greater utility than native DNA (e.g., short sequences used as primers/probes). Usefulness that is merely a consequence of having removed the molecule from its environment (as opposed to new functional properties) is weaker support for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification / 'different in kind' doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Purification can render a natural product patent-eligible if the purification produces a substance that is different 'in kind' — i.e., has new structural features or operative properties — from the impure natural material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (e.g., purified aspirin, Parke-Davis) show purified substances may be eligible where purification yields therapeutic/functional differences. But labeling mere isolation as 'purification' is insufficient unless the product exhibits new in-kind properties beyond being separable from its surroundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA-specific test: synthesized and not occurring in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA molecules, being synthesized to contain contiguous exon sequences and lacking introns, generally do not occur in nature and thus are human-made inventions eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because creation of cDNA requires synthesis from mRNA and significant manipulation, cDNA is treated as an artificial DNA molecule with different sequence/structure and utility. cDNA patents do not risk preempting the use of native genomic DNA in the same way isolated genomic DNA claims might.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether claim would 'tie up' essential prerequisite for study/use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention is simply the necessary consequence of removing a natural product from its environment (a prerequisite to study/use), granting a patent may unlawfully 'tie up' the underlying natural resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When isolation is required before any meaningful use, treating the isolated form as patent-eligible would effectively grant control over the natural substance itself; courts should decline to do so to avoid preemption (Mayo reasoning applied to compositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO practice and congressional inaction are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding PTO practice of issuing patents on isolated DNA, or Congress's failure to amend the Patent Act, do not by themselves make isolated DNA patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO guidelines (e.g., 2001 Utility Examination Guidelines) lack force of law; congressional inaction or introduction of bills without clear consideration of the precise issue is an unreliable indicator. Reliance interests are weaker absent entrenched judicial precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific incentive arguments insufficient to override §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy arguments about the biotechnology industry's dependence on patents cannot, by themselves, override the judicially-created product-of-nature exception to §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should apply general legal rules balancing innovation incentives and the public interest rather than creating industry-specific exceptions; tailoring to particular industries is for Congress, not the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility of methods and altered products
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a natural product itself is not patent-eligible, novel methods of identifying, isolating, or using that product, and human-made alterations of that product, can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to new processes or to materially altered products (not merely isolated native products) remain viable paths to protection. Courts should distinguish composition claims that monopolize the natural product from method/alteration claims that amount to human inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest balancing and the 'two-edged sword' principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection must be balanced against the public interest in free access to natural laws and substances because patents can impede flow of information and raise costs of using fundamental natural resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing §101 eligibility, consider social costs of exclusivity and whether an overly broad interpretation would unduly restrict study and exploitation of natural resources; public interest considerations weigh against granting patents that effectively monopolize natural phenomena.
